78.title: Mecca, a valley of trade and idols
78.hook: the old House of Ibrahim stands in a dry valley ringed with idols, and the tribe of Quraysh keeps it
78.howItsDone: Muslims face the Ka'ba in Mecca in every prayer, and travel there for hajj and 'umrah, walking around the House that Muslims believe Ibrahim and Isma'il built.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yaqtin, the gourd vine over a sick prophet, and the city he gave up on. Your line was the city believed. Did you take one step back toward something you left? Day seventy-eight.

Go back to day forty-two. Ibrahim and his son Isma'il, in a dry valley between bare hills, lifting stones, building a simple house for the worship of one God, and praying: our Lord, accept it from us. Now jump forward, many centuries. Same valley. Same house, the Ka'ba. But look around it now. Idols, standing around the house built for One. Caravans rolling in loaded with goods. Poets, traders, pilgrims, deals being struck. This is Mecca, just before the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is born. For the next few weeks, this path follows his life, starting here.
screen: `A HOUSE BUILT FOR ONE.` → `CENTURIES LATER: IDOLS AROUND IT.` → `THIS IS MECCA.`

segments.voice: Mecca, or Makkah, sits in a valley where almost nothing grows. The Qur'an remembers Ibrahim praying for it as a valley without crops, next to Allah's sacred House. So why would anyone live there? Two reasons: water, from the well of Zamzam that you met with Hajar on day forty, and the House itself. Pilgrims came to visit the Ka'ba, and where pilgrims come, trade comes. The tribe that kept the House was Quraysh. They ran the pilgrim trade, fed and watered visitors, and sent caravans out; commentators say south toward Yemen in winter and north toward Syria in summer. A short surah, the hundred and sixth, names Quraysh and their winter and summer journeys, and then tells them, in Pickthall's words: “So let them worship the Lord of this House.” The Lord of this House. Not the idols. Because by now, the house of Ibrahim was crowded with them. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says that years later, there were three hundred and sixty idols around the Ka'ba. The Qur'an names three goddesses worshiped there: al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat. Muslims call this age the jahiliyyah, the time of not knowing. But not everyone had forgotten. A few people in Mecca, called hanifs, turned away from the idols and tried to follow the religion of Ibrahim, as best they knew it. So picture the valley: a trading town, rich and proud, clever with poetry and deals, with an old house at its center, still standing, still visited, still waiting to be what it was built for.
screen: `A VALLEY WITHOUT CROPS.` · `QURAYSH: WINTER AND SUMMER CARAVANS.` · `THE LORD OF THIS HOUSE.` · `A FEW HANIFS REMEMBERED.` · then, large: `A HOUSE WAITING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: picture a place you know, before it changed. Settle, and breathe. A grandparent's house before it was sold. Your street before the new buildings. A church, mosque or temple before it was renovated. A room before someone moved out. Walk through it slowly in your mind. What did it smell like? What was it for? Now notice what it's for now. Some things change on the outside and keep their purpose. Some lose it and wait. If you pray, you can remember that place with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Mecca. Makkah: the dry valley of Ibrahim's House, a trading town kept by Quraysh, crowded with idols, where the Prophet ﷺ would be born.

Your line: a house waiting. Today, notice one thing in your life that's been waiting to be used for what it's really for: a gift, a room, an hour. Tomorrow, an army with an elephant. Day seventy-eight.

79.title: The year of the elephant
79.hook: an army with an elephant marches on the Ka'ba and is turned back, in the year the Prophet ﷺ is born
79.howItsDone: Surah Al-Fil is a short surah often recited in prayer; the Year of the Elephant is remembered as the year of the Prophet's birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mecca: a dry valley, a trading tribe, and the House of Ibrahim ringed with idols. Your line was a house waiting. What in your life is waiting? Day seventy-nine.

Over the hills south of Mecca comes an army. Soldiers, banners, dust. And at the front of it, an elephant. A living mountain, walking. The army has come for one reason: to tear down the Ka'ba. Its commander, a man named Abraha, governor of Yemen, had built a grand house of worship in his own city, and he wanted the pilgrims of Arabia to go there instead. So he's come to knock down the competition. The Meccans are traders, not soldiers. They look at the elephant, and they head for the hills.
screen: `AN ARMY FROM THE SOUTH.` → `IN FRONT: AN ELEPHANT.` → `THE MECCANS HEAD FOR THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: The early biography of the Prophet, by Ibn Ishaq, tells what happened next. Abraha's soldiers seize two hundred camels belonging to the chief of Mecca, an old man named 'Abd al-Muttalib. So 'Abd al-Muttalib goes to meet Abraha, and Abraha is impressed: a dignified man. Surely he's come to plead for the Ka'ba. But 'Abd al-Muttalib asks only for his camels. Abraha is disappointed. You came about camels, and not the house of your fathers' religion? And the old man answers, in the words the story remembers: I am the owner of the camels. The House has its own Lord, who will protect it. Then the elephant, the story says, kneels down facing Mecca and will not get up. Turn it toward Yemen, it walks. Turn it toward the Ka'ba, it sits. And the Qur'an tells the rest in a short surah, the hundred and fifth, called Al-Fil, the Elephant. In Pickthall's translation it begins: “Hast thou not seen how thy Lord dealt with the owners of the Elephant?” Allah sent against them, it says, “swarms of flying creatures,” pelting them with stones of baked clay, until they were like chewed-up straw. The army is broken, and the House stands. Tradition says the Arabs dated years from it: the Year of the Elephant. And in that same year, Ibn Ishaq says, a boy was born in Mecca into 'Abd al-Muttalib's own family. His grandson. His name was Muhammad ﷺ. Muslim tradition sees the timing as a sign: the House is protected, and the one who will restore it to the worship of One God is born.
screen: `ONLY THE CAMELS, PLEASE.` · `THE ELEPHANT KNEELS.` · `SWARMS OF FLYING CREATURES.` · `THE YEAR A BOY IS BORN.` · then, large: `THE HOUSE HAS AN OWNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand under the sky for one breath. If you can, step outside, or go to a window and look up. Take one long breath in, and let it out slowly. Notice how big it is up there, and how small the things that frighten you look against it. Then sit, wherever you are, and let the rest of the time be quiet. You don't have to protect everything yourself. If you pray, you can hand one worry to the Lord of the House. The bell holds the time.
Al-feel, the elephant: the animal at the front of the army that could not be moved to tear down the Ka'ba.
Your line: the house has an owner. Today, when you're tempted to carry something that isn't yours to carry, say it, and set it down. Tomorrow, the boy grows up an orphan. Day seventy-nine.

80.title: An orphan in the desert
80.hook: his father dies before he is born, and no nurse wants the fatherless baby, until Halimah takes him to the desert
80.howItsDone: Islam asks believers to care for orphans; some Muslims sponsor an orphan through a charity, and Surah Ad-Duha is read as a reminder of the Prophet's own childhood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-feel, the year of the elephant: an army turned back, and a boy born in Mecca. Your line was the house has an owner. What did you set down? Day eighty.

Before the boy was even born, his father was gone. 'Abdullah, a young man, had left on a trading journey, fell ill on the way home, and died. So Aminah gave birth to a son whose father would never hold him. His grandfather named him Muhammad ﷺ. Now, the families of Mecca had a custom. They sent their babies out to the desert tribes, to be nursed by Bedouin women, for the clean air and the pure Arabic. Every so often, women from the desert came into town looking for babies to nurse, because the parents paid well. And that year, not one of them wanted this baby. No father. Who would pay?
screen: `A FATHER GONE BEFORE THE BIRTH.` → `BABIES SENT TO THE DESERT.` → `NOBODY WANTS THE ORPHAN.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq's biography tells it through one of those women. Her name was Halimah, from the tribe of Banu Sa'd. It was a drought year. Her donkey was so weak it held up the whole group. Her own baby cried all night because she barely had milk. Every other woman found a child. Halimah found only the orphan. And rather than go home with nothing, she said to her husband: I'll take him. The story says that from that night everything changed: her milk came in, their old camel gave milk, and her slow donkey ran ahead of the others. The orphan nobody wanted brought blessing into the tent. He grew up out there for several years, running with the flocks, speaking the Arabic of the desert. The Arabic word for him is yatim: an orphan, a child who has lost a father. Years later, the Qur'an would speak to him directly about this. In Surah Ad-Duha, in Pickthall's translation: “Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?” Allah found you an orphan, and sheltered you. And two verses later, the job that comes with it: “Therefor the orphan oppress not.” And orphans come up again and again in the Qur'an. Their property is to be guarded, not devoured. They're to be fed, honored, and never pushed away. And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet ﷺ held up two fingers, side by side, and said that he and the one who cares for an orphan will be like this in Paradise. The boy nobody wanted became the one who told the world to want them.
screen: `HALIMAH, IN A DROUGHT YEAR.` · `SHE TAKES THE ONE LEFT OVER.` · `DID HE NOT FIND THEE AN ORPHAN?` · `THE ORPHAN OPPRESS NOT.` · then, large: `ALLAH SHELTERS THE ORPHAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one kindness for someone alone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's on their own right now. A widowed neighbor. A new kid at school. A coworker who eats lunch at their desk. Someone far from family. Picture their face. What's one small thing that would tell them someone noticed? A knock on the door. A seat saved. A message. Choose it now, so it's ready when the bell ends. If you pray, you can ask Allah to shelter them. The bell holds the time.
Yatim. An orphan, a child who has lost a father. The Prophet ﷺ was one, and the Qur'an asks that every orphan be protected.
Your line: Allah shelters the orphan. Today, do the kindness you chose, for someone alone. Tomorrow, the people who took him in, one after another. Day eighty.

81.title: Mother, grandfather, uncle
81.hook: his mother dies when he is six, his grandfather two years later, and each time someone takes him in
81.howItsDone: Honoring parents is one of the strongest duties in Islam, second in the Qur'an only to worshiping Allah; many Muslims say the prayer of 17:24 for their parents after their daily prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orphan nobody wanted, and Halimah, who took him anyway. Your line was Allah shelters the orphan. Did you find someone alone? Day eighty-one.

He comes back from the desert a little boy, sunburned, speaking the Bedouin Arabic, and he goes home to his mother. Aminah. For a short while, it's the two of them. When he's six, she takes him on a trip north, to the town of Yathrib, to see relatives and to visit the grave of the father he never met. A long camel ride, a mother and her son and a servant woman named Umm Ayman. And on the way home, at a place called al-Abwa', Aminah falls ill. And she dies there, on the road. A six-year-old boy, standing by his mother's grave in the desert, a long way from home.
screen: `HOME TO HIS MOTHER.` → `A TRIP TO HIS FATHER'S GRAVE.` → `AT AL-ABWA', SHE DIES.`

segments.voice: Umm Ayman brings him back to Mecca, and someone takes him in: his grandfather, 'Abd al-Muttalib, the old chief from the story of the elephant. The biography by Ibn Ishaq has a tender detail. 'Abd al-Muttalib had a rug laid out for him in the shade of the Ka'ba, and none of his grown sons would dare sit on it, out of respect. But the little boy would climb right onto it, and when his uncles tried to move him, the old man said: leave him be. Two years later, when the boy is eight, his grandfather dies too. And someone takes him in again: his uncle Abu Talib, a man with many children and not much money, who raises him as his own and will protect him for the rest of his life. Mother. Grandfather. Uncle. Three homes by the age of eight. And the servant woman, Umm Ayman, who stayed with him through all of it; he is reported to have called her his mother after his mother. He never forgot Aminah. A hadith in Sahih Muslim tells how, as a grown man, the Prophet ﷺ visited his mother's grave and wept, and everyone around him wept too. This is part of why Islam speaks of parents and caregivers the way it does. The Qur'an asks believers to be gentle with them as they grow old, and gives a prayer for them, in Pickthall's words: “My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little.” Loss after loss. And each time, somebody opened a door.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who raised you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people who took you in. A parent. A grandparent. An aunt, a coach, a teacher, a neighbor, whoever it really was. Pick one. Picture them at the age they were when they were looking after you. Say thank you, silently, and mean it. If they've died, say it anyway. If you pray, you can use the Qur'an's words: my Lord, have mercy on them both, as they cared for me when I was little. The bell holds the time.
Mother. Umm, in Arabic. Aminah, who died on the road when her son was six, and whose grave he wept at as a grown man.

Your line: someone always took him in. Today, tell one person who took you in, in any way, that you remember. Tomorrow, the boy grows up, and people start trusting him with everything. Day eighty-one.

82.title: Al-Amin, the trustworthy
82.hook: a young shepherd and merchant becomes known in Mecca as the one you leave your valuables with
82.howItsDone: Muslims treat keeping trusts, returning loans, keeping secrets and keeping promises as part of faith itself, and a hadith lists betraying a trust among the signs of a hypocrite.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mother, grandfather, uncle: three homes by the age of eight. Your line was someone always took him in. Did you thank one of yours? Day eighty-two.

House keys make a good test. Not a phone password: the actual keys to your home, handed over for a month while you're away. That list tends to be short. One or two names, if that. In Mecca, one young man's name sat on that kind of list all over town. Not rich, not powerful, an orphan raised by his uncle. And he had a nickname. You met it on day twenty of this path. They called him al-Amin. The trustworthy one. Today, the word behind the nickname.
screen: `WHO GETS YOUR KEYS?` → `ONE NAME ALL OVER TOWN.` → `AL-AMIN.`

segments.voice: The word is amanah: a trust. Something handed to you that isn't yours, that you're expected to keep safe and give back whole. Money left in your care. A secret. A job. A promise. It comes from the root a-m-n, which means to be safe, secure. The same root gives iman, faith, and amin, the trustworthy. So in Arabic, faith, safety and trustworthiness are family. How did he earn the name? Not with speeches. As a boy he herded sheep for Meccan families for a few coins; a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says he told his companions every prophet had been a shepherd. As a young man he traveled with the trade caravans. And the name stuck so hard that, years later, even people in Mecca who opposed him kept leaving their valuables with him. The seerah says that on the night he finally left Mecca, he asked his cousin 'Ali to stay behind and return every one of those deposits to its owner. Even his opponents' things. The Qur'an makes this a command for everyone. In Pickthall's translation: “Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners.” And it goes further. It describes the amanah, the trust, being offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they shrank from carrying it. And the human being took it on. Muslim scholars read that trust in many ways: faith, the body, time, the earth itself. In that reading, everything a person holds is held on loan.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one promise exactly. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you said you'd do. A call you promised. A thing you borrowed. A deadline. An I'll be there at six. Pick one that's still open. Picture keeping it exactly, not roughly, not late, not almost. On time, and whole. Decide when you'll do it today. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make you trustworthy in small things. The bell holds the time.
Amanah. A trust: whatever is placed in your care, to be kept safe and given back whole. The root of al-Amin, the Prophet's name in Mecca.
Your line: be the one they trust. Keep the promise you picked, exactly as you said it. Tomorrow, a businesswoman notices him. Day eighty-two.

83.title: Khadijah hires him
83.hook: a respected merchant hires him, sees his honesty, and proposes marriage
83.tomorrow: the black stone on a cloak
83.howItsDone: Muslims honor Khadijah as the Prophet's first wife, the first to accept Islam, and one of the best of women; her marriage is often held up as a model of loyalty and mutual respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, amanah, a trust, and a young man the whole town called al-Amin. Your line was be the one they trust. Did you keep your promise exactly? Day eighty-three.

In Mecca there was a businesswoman. Not a merchant's wife, a merchant. Her name was Khadijah. She was widowed, wealthy, respected, from a noble family, and she ran her own trading business, hiring men to carry her goods north with the caravans and sell them in Syria. And like any good boss, she paid attention to reputations. She kept hearing one name. The young man they call al-Amin. Honest. Careful. Doesn't cheat. So she sent for him, and offered him a job.
screen: `A MERCHANT, NOT A MERCHANT'S WIFE.` → `SHE HEARS ONE NAME.` → `SHE OFFERS HIM A JOB.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq's biography says she offered him more than she usually paid, and sent her servant Maysarah along on the journey to Syria. He traded her goods and came home with a profit. But what Maysarah told her about the journey, and about the man, mattered more than the money. So she made a decision. Through a friend, she asked whether he would marry her. Tradition says he was about twenty-five, and she about forty; some early reports make her younger. Either way, she was the one who proposed. He accepted, and his uncles arranged the marriage. For as long as she lived, she was his only wife. They had children together: four daughters, Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah, and sons who died as little boys. And years later, after she was gone, he still sent gifts to her old friends, and he's reported in Sahih Muslim to have said simply: I was given her love. The Qur'an describes marriage like this, in Pickthall's words: Allah created mates for you that you might find rest in them, “and He ordained between you love and mercy.” Rest, love, mercy. And here's why today's line matters. Before any angel came to any cave, Khadijah had already seen who he was. She saw him first. Muslim tradition remembers her as the first to accept Islam, and a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari names her among the best of women.
screen: `MAYSARAH REPORTS HIS CHARACTER.` · `SHE PROPOSES.` · `HIS ONLY WIFE WHILE SHE LIVED.` · `I WAS GIVEN HER LOVE.` · then, large: `SHE SAW HIM FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see someone the way Khadijah did. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose good qualities nobody seems to mention. The coworker who quietly fixes things. The relative who always shows up. The friend who keeps their word. Picture them doing the thing nobody thanks them for. Find the plain words for what you see in them: you're honest, you're steady, you're kind. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward them. The bell holds the time.

84.title: The black stone on a cloak
84.word: The black stone on a cloak
84.hook: the clans of Mecca nearly come to blows over who will lift the Black Stone, and he lays it on a cloak so every clan lifts together
84.howItsDone: Pilgrims begin each circuit of the Ka'ba at the Black Stone, kissing or touching it if they can reach it, or raising a hand toward it from a distance; Muslims honor it as a stone the Prophet kissed, not as an object of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khadijah hired him, saw who he was, and asked him to marry her. Your line was she saw him first. Did you tell someone what you see in them? Day eighty-four, the end of week twelve.

Every group project has this moment. The work is almost done, and now there's the part everyone can see, the part that gets the credit, and suddenly everyone wants to do it. In Mecca, around the time the Prophet ﷺ was thirty-five, the Ka'ba had been damaged, and the clans of Quraysh tore it down to its foundations and rebuilt it together, each clan taking a wall. It went well. Until the very last step: setting the Black Stone, the ancient stone in the Ka'ba's corner, back in its place. Every clan wanted the honor. Nobody would back down. Days passed. Swords came out.
screen: `THE KA'BA REBUILT, WALL BY WALL.` → `WHO SETS THE STONE?` → `SWORDS COME OUT.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq tells it. Some clans even dipped their hands in a bowl of blood and swore to fight. Then the oldest man there made a suggestion: let the next man who walks through the gate of the sanctuary decide, and we'll all accept it. They agreed. And the next man through the gate was the young man they called al-Amin. They were relieved. It's the trustworthy one. We accept him. He listened, and then he asked for a cloak. He spread it on the ground and set the Black Stone in the middle of it with his own hands. Then he said: let each clan's leader take hold of a corner. And they lifted it, together, all of them, up to its place. Then he took the stone and set it into the wall. No clan won. Every clan carried. And the man who solved it didn't take the honor for himself; he shared it out. Today Muslims walking around the Ka'ba on pilgrimage kiss the Black Stone, or touch it, or simply raise a hand toward it from the crowd. But it isn't worshiped. A famous report in Sahih al-Bukhari has 'Umar, a leading companion, saying to the stone: I know you're only a stone, you can neither harm nor help; if I hadn't seen the Prophet ﷺ kiss you, I wouldn't kiss you. The Qur'an asks believers, in Pickthall's words: “hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate.” And that closes week twelve: a valley of idols, an elephant, an orphan, three homes, a trust, a merchant who saw him first, and a cloak with four corners.
screen: `HANDS IN A BOWL OF BLOOD.` · `THE NEXT MAN THROUGH THE GATE.` · `A CLOAK, AND EVERY CLAN LIFTS.` · `ONLY A STONE, SAYS 'UMAR.` · then, large: `EVERYONE TAKES A CORNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the solution where everyone carries. Settle, and breathe. Think of one standoff in your life right now. Who does the dishes. Who hosts the holidays. Who gets credit on the team. Picture everyone involved, standing around it. Now look for the cloak: a way for each person to hold a corner, so nobody wins and nobody loses. It doesn't have to be perfect. Just one idea. If you pray, you can ask Allah for a way through. The bell holds the time.
The black stone on a cloak. The clans nearly fight over one honor, and he lays the stone on a cloak so all of them can lift it together.
